sources.title: Connecticut Department of Banking - Rental Security Deposits
Connecticut General Statutes Sec. 47a-21 - Security deposits

rules.title: Security deposit above two months' rent
rules.summary: A Connecticut landlord may not require more than two months' rent as a security deposit for a tenant under 62.
rules.what_to_do: Ask the landlord in writing to bring the deposit within the statutory cap before you sign or send money.

rules.title: Security deposit above one month for a tenant aged 62 or older
rules.summary: For a tenant who is 62 or older the cap drops to one month's rent, and any pet deposit counts toward it.
rules.what_to_do: Tell the landlord the one-month cap applies and ask for a corrected lease.

rules.title: Deposit must sit in a Connecticut escrow account
rules.summary: The deposit must be held in an escrow account at a financial institution located in Connecticut. It is not the landlord's money to spend.
rules.what_to_do: Ask which Connecticut institution holds the escrow account, and keep the answer in writing.

rules.title: Deposit earns interest you are owed
rules.summary: Landlords owe interest on security deposits at a rate the Banking Commissioner publishes each year. Many tenants never ask for it.
rules.what_to_do: At move-out, ask for the deposit plus accrued interest, and check the current published rate.

rules.title: Deposit must come back within 30 days
rules.summary: After the tenancy ends the landlord has 30 days to return the unused deposit with interest, or deliver an itemised list of deductions. A landlord who wrongfully withholds can be liable for twice the amount.
rules.what_to_do: Give a forwarding address in writing at move-out and diarise the 30-day deadline.

rules.title: Pet deposit charged on top of the cap
rules.summary: A pet deposit counts toward the same two-month cap. It cannot be stacked on top of a full security deposit. Service and emotional support animals are exempt from pet charges.
rules.what_to_do: Add the deposits together and check the total against two months' rent.

scam_patterns.title: Money requested before anyone has seen the unit
scam_patterns.summary: Being asked to send money before a viewing, or before a lease exists, is the single most common rental scam against students arriving from abroad.
scam_patterns.what_to_do: Never send money before a signed lease and a live video walkthrough of the actual unit.

scam_patterns.title: Cash, wire, gift card, or crypto demanded
scam_patterns.summary: Untraceable payment methods are demanded precisely because they cannot be reversed.
scam_patterns.what_to_do: Insist on a method that leaves a record and is reversible.

scam_patterns.title: Landlord claims to be out of the country
scam_patterns.summary: A landlord who cannot meet, cannot show the unit, and wants the keys mailed is a standard scam script.
scam_patterns.what_to_do: Require a viewing by the landlord, an agent, or a current tenant before any payment.

scam_patterns.title: Priced far below everything else nearby
scam_patterns.summary: A unit priced well under the neighbourhood baseline is more often a fake listing than a bargain.
scam_patterns.what_to_do: Verify the address exists, is actually for rent, and that the person has the right to rent it.

scam_patterns.title: No written lease offered
scam_patterns.summary: Without a written lease you have very little you can enforce, and no document to show an immigration or financial-aid office.
scam_patterns.what_to_do: Ask for the written lease before paying anything.

ambiguous_terms.why: An electricity allowance with a 'reasonable cap' does not say what the cap is in dollars. Overage is billed to the tenant.
Rarely means all of them. Ask which specific utilities, by name.
Does not imply hot water or cooking gas are included.
May mean the lease starts immediately, charging you for months before you arrive.
